people.seed: Anglican choir member, 60, Yorkshire, loves old churches and quiet
people.desc: Margaret Hinchcliffe, a retired primary school teacher from a village outside Skipton, has sung alto in her parish choir for thirty-one years and would rather sing Evensong to six people than attend a praise night. Her faith is steady but unshowy: she says the Creed every week, is privately unsure about hell, and keeps a copy of Julian of Norwich by the bed. She is dry, reserved and quick to laugh, and has no patience for people who tell others how to live. She nursed her mother through a long dementia and still visits the churchyard most Sundays after the service.

notes.note: She loves an empty church on a weekday, but the choir is where she feels most held. It is both for her, so she chose Not sure.
She agrees you ought to give it away, but 'really belongs to them' sounds like a slogan. She has no answer for 'ought to' versus 'belongs', so Not sure.
She lives with an established church and never thinks about it. The statement sounds American to her, and she could not say whether that arrangement counts.
She hopes so rather than believes it. Agree is the nearest she can get to 'I would like to think so'.
She thinks 'it depends on the family and on the calling'. Not sure is honest but a bit of a dodge.

people.overall: Pleasant and easy; it felt more like a chat over tea than a test of doctrine. She would have liked a 'hope so' answer for the one about everyone being saved.

people.seed: Former atheist, now Catholic, 35, Chicago, corporate lawyer
people.desc: Daniel Reyes grew up in a secular household in Evanston, was a confident atheist through college, and was received into the Catholic Church at an Easter Vigil at 29 after reading Aquinas and Chesterton to argue against them. He is a litigation associate at a Loop firm, argues for a living, and reads theology on the train the way other people read sports news. His parents were hurt by his conversion and still treat it as a phase. He is precise to the point of pedantry and cannot answer a question without noticing its hidden premise, but he also cries easily at weddings and funerals, which surprises people.

notes.note: He knows the Church's answer is no, from Augustine and the Catechism, but his gut says yes for the murderer at the door. He picked Not sure because he does not want to disagree with the Church on the record.

He knows the universal destination of goods and the line from the Fathers about bread belonging to the hungry. 'Really belongs to them' is stronger than he is comfortable with as a lawyer who deals in property.
Found it slightly loaded by 'as much as'. You can know that God exists from nature but not the Trinity, so he disagreed with the comparison rather than with nature.
Excommunication exists and he thinks it is medicinal, but 'put out' sounds harsher and more final than what he means.
'We may hope that all are saved' is his real view. 'Will' is a claim he cannot make, so he disagreed, but lightly.
He has read about integralism and finds it interesting but not persuasive. The Church's own teaching on religious freedom holds him back from agreeing.

people.overall: He enjoyed it and wanted to argue with half the statements, which he took as a good sign. He found himself wishing he could add a footnote to several answers.

people.desc: Jess Albrecht grew up Methodist in suburban Ohio, drifted away in college, and found yoga during a rough stretch of panic attacks at 24. She now teaches vinyasa and leads weekend retreats near Ojai, keeps a dream journal, and uses 'God', 'Spirit' and 'the universe' more or less interchangeably. She is warm and a little conflict-averse, but she marches every year for climate causes and can get properly angry about it. She still hums hymns from her childhood when she is cooking and has not quite admitted to herself that she misses church.

notes.note: She agrees about solitude and meditation, but 'God' is not quite her word, so she translated it in her head.
On first read it sounded like equanimity, which she teaches. Then 'never stir' made her disagree: equanimity is not numbness, and feelings should move through you.
She thought of leaving a career her parents wanted in order to teach. 'God is calling you' is not how she would put it, but the answer is still yes.
She is not a Christian, so she answered from the outside and from her own lean toward nonviolence. It felt slightly like it was not her question.
She does not belong to a church, so she answered it as a general principle. Kicking people out sounded like the kind of church she left.
'Save' is not her word. She believes everyone returns to the source, which she took as close enough to agree.

people.overall: Surprisingly easy to take as someone outside church. Most statements felt like things a thoughtful person could agree or disagree with, and only a few assumed she was a Christian.

people.desc: Dr. Mina Girgis came from Alexandria at 22 to finish dental training, and now owns two practices in Hudson County. He serves as a deacon at his parish, keeps the Coptic fasts (well over two hundred days a year), and reads the Sayings of the Desert Fathers in Arabic before bed. He is careful, formal with strangers and funny with family, and he lost a cousin in the 2017 Palm Sunday church bombing in Egypt. He is proud of his business sense and sees no contradiction between fasting strictly and driving a nice car.

notes.note: The monks go to the desert, but the Liturgy is the heart of everything and it is never alone. He cannot choose one over the other.
He thinks the body is a temple, but fasting is a discipline and St Paul says 'I discipline my body'. The statement makes him pick between two things he holds together.
The stories happened AND they have a deeper meaning. He disagreed because 'more than what literally happened' sounded like doubting them.
He believes in working together with God's grace. 'Mostly up to you' is half true and half wrong, so Not sure.
He did military service in Egypt and does not condemn soldiers, but 'a clear conscience' about killing sits badly with him. Not sure.
Living as a minority where the state backs another religion made him wary of any government deciding faith. In America he might feel differently, so the answer depends on which government.
He gives generously and knows St John Chrysostom on this, but he worked hard for what he has. 'Really belongs to them' pulled him both ways.
He read it as the Fathers' dispassion and agreed, though he wondered whether the quiz meant something colder.

people.overall: Respectful, and he liked that nothing mocked belief. Several statements split things his Church holds together, so he kept wanting an 'both are true' button.

people.seed: Sixteen-year-old in an Assemblies of God youth group, Florida
people.desc: Jayden Morales lives in Lakeland, plays drums in his youth group's Wednesday night worship band, and spoke in tongues for the first time at summer camp when he was fourteen. His parents came from Puerto Rico and his grandma prays for him out loud every time he leaves the house. He is loud, loyal and funny, plays a lot of Fortnite, and secretly worries about his best friend from school who says he doesn't believe in anything. He answers fast and goes with his gut.

notes.note: He knows lying is a sin, then thought of Rahab hiding the spies and got stuck. Not sure.
Confusing to him: he did not know what 'the extra really belongs to them' means. He went Not sure because he did not get it, not because he was torn.
A bit confusing ('strong feelings never stir it'), but he figured it meant never getting emotional, and worship at his church is emotional, so he disagreed.
He thought 'America was founded on God, so yes', but did not really know what 'support' would mean in practice.
His church says hell is real, but he thought of his best friend and did not want to answer Strongly. So just Disagree.
His youth pastor warns about worldly wisdom, but his grandpa is not a Christian and is the wisest person he knows.
Felt a little like a trick question, because the answer at his church is 'it's all Jesus', but he still thinks you have to try.

people.overall: Quick and kind of fun, like the questions youth group asks at retreats. A couple of words were too grown-up, but most of it made sense straight away.
